questions.question: Explain the principle of specificity and give a sporting example.

points.text: Specificity means training should be matched to the needs of the sport and the individual. Training must focus on the specific fitness components and movements required. Example: a sprinter should train for speed and power (sprint drills, plyometrics, weight training), not cardiovascular endurance through long slow distance running.

questions.question: What is progressive overload and why is it necessary?

points.text: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the demands of training over time so the body continues to adapt. It is necessary because if training remains the same, the body adapts to the stimulus and reaches a plateau where no further improvements occur. By progressively increasing the load, the body is forced to keep adapting.

questions.question: Explain the principle of reversibility and how it affects an injured athlete.

points.text: Reversibility means training adaptations are lost when training stops or is significantly reduced ("use it or lose it"). An injured athlete who cannot train will lose fitness: cardiovascular endurance declines within 2-3 weeks, muscle atrophy begins within 1-2 weeks, and skill levels deteriorate. questions.question: Define each letter of the FITT principle.

points.text: F = Frequency (how often you train); I = Intensity (how hard you train); T = Time (how long you train); T = Type (what kind of training you do).

questions.question: How could a weightlifter apply the FITT principle to progressively overload their training?

points.text: Frequency: increase from 3 to 4 sessions per week. Intensity: increase the weight on the bar (e.g. from 80kg to 85kg on bench press). Time: increase the duration of sessions or add more sets. Type: vary exercises to target different muscle groups or change from heavy strength work to power-focused work.

questions.question: Explain the difference between SPORT and FITT.

points.text: SPORT describes the overall principles of training (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Overload, Reversibility, Tedium) - the WHY and WHAT. FITT describes how to apply progressive overload in practice (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) - the HOW. FITT is the practical method for implementing the SPORT principle of progressive overload.
